meta.title: Almost nobody sees one fall — how the meteorite catalogue is really made

core_claim: The 45,716-row Meteoritical Bulletin is not a record of meteorites that fell, but a record of meteorites that humans found — 97.6% as later Finds, 59% lifted off Antarctic ice, 97% catalogued after 1969 when systematic searches began. Every other pattern follows from that.

story_spine.tension: Readers assume the catalogue is roughly what hits Earth, sampled by witnesses. In fact only 2.42% were ever seen falling.
story_spine.payoff: The catalogue is mostly an inventory of human attention — which search programs ran, where, and for how long.

edt_01.label: Hook — Almost nobody sees one fall
edt_01.title: Almost nobody sees one fall
edt_01.editorial_notes: Headline numbers 2.42% and ~6 falls/year must be exact. Image hint: the immovable Hoba meteorite (ref_hoba.jpg) — a 60-ton iron block sitting in Namibia for 80,000 years sets the tone that meteorites are physical objects we mostly fail to witness.

edt_02.label: The Find explosion of 1969
edt_02.title: The Find explosion of 1969
edt_02.editorial_notes: The decade pivot chart should show Fell and Found as two stacked or paired bars per decade — Fell stays flat, Found explodes after 1970. Antarctic recovery image (ref_antarctic_recovery.jpg) belongs here. 30x ratio and 17,698 (2000s decade) numbers must be exact.

edt_03.label: A map of where humans looked
edt_03.title: A map of where humans looked
edt_03.editorial_notes: Centrepiece. Use the all-1,097 Fells (red) + 2,000-sample Founds (blue) on a world map. Antarctic and desert hotspots must be unmistakable. Weave in ana_caveat_01: 16% of rows lack coordinates and the map silently drops them.

edt_04.label: Ten orders of magnitude, log-normal
edt_04.title: Ten orders of magnitude, log-normal
edt_04.editorial_notes: Log-bucket histogram. The 92x median-mass gap (Fell vs Found) and the 400x mean-to-median ratio are the headline numbers. Text-only is correct here — a chart of bars on log scale is the strongest visual.

edt_05.label: The top 20 are a wall of iron
edt_05.title: The top 20 are a wall of iron
edt_05.editorial_notes: Top-20 leaderboard with bars or numeric blocks. Image: ref_ahnighito.jpg (Cape York's 34-t fragment at AMNH) is the strongest single image — it shows a real heavyweight at human scale. Rank-19 reveal (Jilin chondrite) is the rhetorical punch.

edt_06.label: Counts say chondrite, mass says iron
edt_06.title: Counts say chondrite, mass says iron
edt_06.editorial_notes: Twin-chart opportunity: family-by-count and family-by-median-mass side by side, showing the rank flip. The lunar 0% Fell observation in ana_12 is the closer — every lunar meteorite in the catalogue came from Antarctica or a desert, none was ever seen falling.

edt_07.label: Close — The catalogue is a record of where we looked
edt_07.title: The catalogue is a record of where we looked
edt_07.editorial_notes: Closer should tie the three load-bearing numbers back together (2.4% witnessed, 59% Antarctic, 97% post-1969). Image: ref_meteor_crater.jpg — the only entry in the catalogue you can still see from orbit. Mention ana_caveat_02 (dataset frozen ~2013) as the reason the 2010s row dips.
